title: Nvidia and Kioxia 1.1PB SSD Memory Experiment Could Transform AI Infrastructure
content:
There’s a quiet revolution happening at the hardware layer, and it’s not about faster chips, it’s about where data lives. NVIDIA and Kioxia just disclosed an experiment that could fundamentally shift how engineers think about memory hierarchy in large-scale AI systems. Result? A single 18-node cluster with over a petabyte of addressable memory, built not from expensive HBM, but from NVMe SSDs sitting right inside each node.
That’s not a typo. We’re talking about petabyte-scale memory from storage.
In November 2026, NVIDIA and Kioxia conducted tests on an 18-node GB200 NVL72 system, equipping each node with a 60TB Kioxia NVMe SSD. Result expanded the system’s total addressable memory capacity by 1.1PB. Builds directly on NVIDIA’s Storage-Next initiative, which the company launched in December 2024 to explore mapping SSD storage directly into a GPU’s memory address space, effectively letting GPUs reach into SSDs as if they were just another tier of memory.
Core idea is straightforward: combine the raw speed of HBM with the enormous capacity of SSD storage to create a virtual memory pool at petabyte scale. It’s a tiered architecture, yes, but one where the boundaries between “fast memory” and “storage” start to blur in meaningful ways.
Worth noting: offloading to SSD isn’t a novel concept. Inference frameworks have been shipping expert weights to SSDs for years, taking advantage of sparsity in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. Google’s Switch-C model card, submitted in November 2022, was among the earliest documented examples. Baidu’s SE-MoE approach did the same during training as far back as May 2022.
What’s different now is the ambition of the architecture. NVIDIA isn’t just routing overflow weights to an SSD, it’s building infrastructure where the GPU’s address space includes the SSD. A fundamentally different design philosophy, and the NVIDIA-Kioxia disclosure suggests the hardware ecosystem is now ready to support it at serious scale.
Here’s where it gets interesting. Today’s largest LLM weights have only reached the terabyte scale, so this technology isn’t primarily aimed at running bigger models on a single node at least not yet. But consider the adjacent use case: vector databases.
A petabyte-scale memory pool could store an extraordinary volume of embedded data. Theoretically, you could index the full text of every book ever published illustrations included, in a single system. That’s not a distant scenario; it’s an engineering target that this architecture makes plausible for the first time.
For enterprises building retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, implications are significant. Latency-sensitive retrieval over massive corpora has always required painful trade-offs between cost, speed, and coverage. A GPU-addressable petabyte pool collapses some of those trade-offs entirely.
None of this matters without the right storage hardware, which is precisely why the NVIDIA-Kioxia partnership is worth watching. Kioxia brings NVMe expertise and the raw capacity; NVIDIA brings the memory address space mapping and the GPU ecosystem. Together, they’re building the plumbing for a memory tier that didn’t exist two years ago.
Whether this becomes a standard deployment pattern depends on cost curves, software maturity, and workload adoption, none of which are guaranteed. Memory wall isn’t being torn down, it’s being extended — one NVMe drive at a time.

report.summary: NVIDIA and Kioxia demonstrated an 18-node GB200 NVL72 cluster with 60TB NVMe SSDs per node, adding 1.1PB of GPU-addressable memory and blurring the line between storage and memory.
report.background: Large AI systems are increasingly bottlenecked not by compute but by the 'memory wall' — HBM capacity per GPU grows slowly and costs enormously, while model weights, KV caches and vector indexes keep expanding. Offloading cold data to SSDs is not new: Mixture-of-Experts frameworks such as Google's Switch-C and Baidu's SE-MoE have shipped expert weights to storage since 2022, and inference engines spill KV cache to host memory or disk. What is new is ambition. NVIDIA's Storage-Next initiative, launched in December 2024, aims to map NVMe drives directly into a GPU's virtual address space via GPUDirect Storage-style paths, so the GPU can page data from SSD as if it were another memory tier rather than an external device. Kioxia supplies the high-capacity NVMe silicon. The experiment is a proof point that the hardware ecosystem — PCIe bandwidth, controller firmware, software stacks — can now support petabyte-scale tiering at rack level.
key_points: Scale achieved: each of 18 GB200 NVL72 nodes carried a 60TB Kioxia NVMe SSD, adding roughly 1.1PB of addressable capacity without buying more HBM — a capacity jump that is simply impossible to match with conventional GPU memory budgets.

Architectural shift: rather than treating SSDs as block storage behind a filesystem, the design places them inside the GPU's address space, creating a tiered pool where HBM handles hot data and flash absorbs the long tail. The boundary between 'memory' and 'storage' becomes a policy decision, not a hardware one.

Historical continuity: SSD offloading for sparse MoE weights dates to 2022 (Google Switch-C, Baidu SE-MoE). The difference now is systemic — mapping the whole device into address space at rack scale, rather than per-framework workarounds for weight overflow.

The real target is vector databases: current LLM weights are only terabyte-scale, so 1.1PB is overkill for model inference. The compelling use case is storing and retrieving billions of embeddings for RAG, collapsing the usual cost/latency/coverage trade-offs.

Adoption is not guaranteed: the economics depend on NVMe price curves, PCIe/CXL bandwidth per GPU, and immature software — page-fault handling, prefetching, coherence and eviction policies are still active research, not production defaults.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this validates a third memory tier between HBM and network storage, potentially easing HBM supply pressure and reshaping data-center design around flash-heavy racks rather than DRAM-heavy ones. For developers, the payoff is architectural: RAG systems could hold corpus-scale embeddings in one addressable pool, and inference engines gain a cheap place to spill KV cache and inactive experts — but only if frameworks like vLLM, SGLang and vector databases expose the tier cleanly, otherwise the complexity lands on application code. For regular users, the near-term effect is indirect: larger effective context, better retrieval accuracy on niche or long-tail queries, and cheaper serving of big models, rather than a visible product change. The memory wall is being extended, not removed — expect hybrid designs, not HBM's replacement.
report.tools: Watch NVIDIA's Storage-Next and GPUDirect Storage documentation, plus cuFile APIs for direct device-to-GPU paths. On the storage side, Kioxia's high-capacity data-center NVMe lines (CM/LC series) and comparable drives from Solidigm and Samsung. For software experimentation, try vLLM or SGLang with KV-cache offloading, LMCache for cache tiering, and DeepSpeed-Inference/FlexGen for weight offload research; pair with Milvus, Qdrant or FAISS to test petabyte-scale vector retrieval.
